thinking_and_logic: The submitted approach iterates through nums and collects indices where nums[i] == target. That logic solves a different problem (finding elements equal to target) and never considers pairs or complements, so it cannot satisfy tests where the answer requires nums[i] + nums[j] == target, including duplicates and negative numbers.
code_assessment: Compared with the answer key’s optimal solution (single-pass hash map of seen values -> index, checking complement before inserting), your code is missing the core technique: complement lookup. The canonical approach guarantees finding the unique pair in O(n) time by checking whether target - nums[i] has been seen; your implementation does not compute complements and therefore returns [] for virtually all valid Two Sum instances.

next_steps.action: Implement Two Sum using the single-pass hash map (complement lookup) pattern.
next_steps.why: It matches the problem definition and achieves the optimal O(n) time expected by the answer key for up to 1e5 elements.
next_steps.how: Maintain dict seen = {value: index}. For each i,val: comp = target - val; if comp in seen: return [seen[comp], i]; else seen[val] = i.

next_steps.action: Add a 30-second pre-code validation habit: restate the requirement + run one hand-worked example.
next_steps.why: This prevents common pitfalls listed in the answer key (misreading as equality, using same element twice) and catches spec mismatches early.
next_steps.how: Say/write: 'Need two distinct indices i!=j with sum==target.' Then test mentally on [2,7,11,15], 9 and on a duplicate case like [3,3], 6.

next_steps.action: Practice 3–5 problems that are “hash map for complement / pair sum” variants.
next_steps.why: It builds automatic recognition of when to use seen/complement, and improves speed under time pressure.
next_steps.how: Do: Two Sum, Two Sum II (sorted, two pointers), 3Sum (sort + two pointers), Subarray Sum Equals K (prefix-sum hash map), and validate returned indices vs values each time.
